paragraphs: I can’t say whether the President split the witnesses for the defense and for the prosecution into groups, or arranged to call them in any set order. No doubt he did. All I know is that the witnesses for the prosecution came first. Again, I don’t mean to go through the questioning step by step. My account would be partly pointless anyway, because the speeches for the prosecution and for the defense pulled the whole course of the evidence together and showed it in a strong, telling light. I took down parts of those two remarkable speeches in full, and I will quote them in their place. I will also tell of one extraordinary and quite unexpected episode that came before the final speeches, and that surely helped bring about the sinister, fatal outcome of the trial.

I will only point out one odd feature of the case that was plain to everyone from the first moments of the trial: the prosecution was overwhelmingly stronger than anything the defense had to lean on. Everyone saw it as soon as the facts began to gather around a single point and the whole horrible, bloody crime came gradually into view. Perhaps everyone felt from the start that the case was beyond dispute, that there was no doubt in it, that there could really be no argument, that the defense was a mere formality, and that the prisoner was guilty, plainly and conclusively guilty. I imagine that even the ladies, so impatient to see the interesting prisoner acquitted, were all of them, at the same time, convinced of his guilt. What’s more, I believe they would have been mortified if his guilt had not been so firmly proved, because that would have weakened the effect of the closing scene, when the criminal is acquitted. Strange to say, all the ladies were firmly sure right up to the last moment that he would be acquitted. “He is guilty, but he will be acquitted, out of humanity, in keeping with the new ideas and the new feelings that have come into fashion,” and so on, and so on. That was why they had crowded into the court so eagerly. The men cared more about the contest between the prosecutor and the famous Fetyukovitch. They kept asking themselves what even a talent like Fetyukovitch’s could make of such a hopeless case, and so they followed his every move with close attention.

Yet Fetyukovitch stayed a riddle to everyone until the very end, until his speech. Experienced people suspected that he had a design, that he was working toward some aim, but it was almost impossible to guess what. His confidence and self-reliance were unmistakable, though. Everyone noticed, too, and was pleased, that after so short a stay among us, perhaps no more than three days, he had mastered the case so wonderfully and “had studied it to the last detail.” Afterward people described with relish how cleverly he had “taken down” all the witnesses for the prosecution. He had confused them as much as he could and, what’s more, had smeared their reputations and so lowered the worth of their evidence. But people supposed he did this rather as sport, so to speak, for professional glory, to show that none of the accepted methods had been skipped. They were all convinced that blackening the witnesses like this could do him no real good, and that he knew it better than anyone. They thought he had some idea of his own in reserve, some hidden weapon of defense, which he would spring on us when the time came. Meanwhile, sure of his strength, he seemed to be amusing himself.

For example, when Grigory, Fyodor Pavlovitch’s old servant, gave evidence, the counsel for the defense simply pounced on him when his turn to ask questions came. Grigory was the one who had given the most damning testimony about the open door. It should be said that he walked into the hall calm and almost stately, not in the least put off by the majesty of the court or the huge audience listening to him. He gave his evidence as confidently as if he were chatting with his Marfa, only perhaps more respectfully. There was no making him contradict himself. The prosecutor questioned him first, at length, about the family life of the Karamazovs. The family portrait came out in lurid colors. You could see and hear that the witness was honest and fair. Despite his deep reverence for his dead master’s memory, he still testified that the old man had been unjust to Mitya and “hadn’t brought up his children as he should. He’d have been eaten alive by lice when he was little, if it hadn’t been for me,” he added, speaking of Mitya’s early childhood. “It wasn’t right either, a father cheating his son over his mother’s property, which was his by rights.”

The prosecutor asked what grounds he had for saying that Fyodor Pavlovitch had wronged his son in money matters. To everyone’s surprise, Grigory had no proof whatever to offer. Still, he insisted that the settlement with the son was “unfair” and that the father ought “to have paid him several thousand roubles more.” I should mention, by the way, that the prosecutor pressed this question, whether Fyodor Pavlovitch had really held back part of Mitya’s inheritance, on every witness who could be asked it, Alyosha and Ivan included. But he got no exact information from anyone. All said it was so, and none could produce any clear proof. Grigory’s account of the scene at the dinner table, when Dmitri burst in, beat his father and threatened to come back and kill him, left a sinister impression on the court. The old servant told it calmly, sparing his words, in his own odd way of speaking, and that was as effective as eloquence. He said he was not angry with Mitya for knocking him down and hitting him in the face. He had forgiven him long ago. Of the late Smerdyakov he said, crossing himself, that he was a gifted lad, but stupid and afflicted, and, worse still, a godless one, and that Fyodor Pavlovitch and his elder son had taught him to be so. But he defended Smerdyakov’s honesty almost warmly. He told how Smerdyakov had once found the master’s money in the yard and, instead of hiding it, had carried it to his master. The master had given him a “gold piece” for it and trusted him completely from then on. He insisted stubbornly that the garden door had been open. But he was asked so many questions that I can’t remember them all.

At last the counsel for the defense began his cross-examination. His first question concerned the envelope in which Fyodor Pavlovitch was supposed to have put three thousand roubles for “a certain person.” “Did you ever see it, you who attended your master so closely for so many years?” Grigory answered that he had not seen it, and had never heard of the money from anyone “till everybody was talking about it.” Fetyukovitch asked this question about the envelope of everyone who could conceivably have known of it, just as persistently as the prosecutor asked his about Dmitri’s inheritance, and he got the same answer from all: nobody had seen the envelope, though many had heard of it. From the beginning everyone noticed how Fetyukovitch kept coming back to this subject.

“Now, if you’ll allow me, I’ll ask you something,” Fetyukovitch said, suddenly and unexpectedly. “What was that balsam made of—or rather that decoction—which, as we learn from the preliminary inquiry, you rubbed on your lumbago that evening, hoping to cure it?”
Grigory stared blankly at him. After a short silence he muttered, “There was saffron in it.”
“Only saffron? You don’t remember anything else in it?”
“Milfoil, too.”
“And pepper, maybe?” Fetyukovitch asked.
“Yes, pepper too.”
“And so on. And all of it dissolved in vodka?”
“In spirit.”
A faint ripple of laughter ran through the court.
“You see, in spirit. And after rubbing your back, I believe, you drank what was left in the bottle, saying a certain pious prayer that only your wife knows?”
“I did.”
“Did you drink much? A glass or two, roughly?”
“Could have been a tumblerful.”
“A tumblerful, then. Maybe a tumbler and a half?”
Grigory didn’t answer. He seemed to see what was being aimed at.
“A glass and a half of neat spirit—not bad at all, is it? You could see the gates of heaven open, not just the door into the garden?”
Grigory kept silent. Again there was laughter in the court. The President shifted in his seat.
“And do you know for certain,” Fetyukovitch pressed on, “whether you were awake or not when you saw the open door?”
“I was standing up.”
“That doesn’t prove you were awake.” (Again there was laughter in the court.) “If someone had asked you a question at that moment, could you have answered it? What year it is, for instance?”
“I don’t know.”
“And what year is it, Anno Domini? Do you know?”
Grigory stood there bewildered, looking straight at his tormentor. Strange to say, he really did seem not to know the year.
“Then perhaps you can tell me how many fingers you have on your hands?”
“I am a servant,” Grigory said suddenly, in a loud, clear voice. “If my betters want to make sport of me, it is my duty to bear it.”

Fetyukovitch was slightly taken aback. The President stepped in and told him to keep his questions to the point. Fetyukovitch bowed with dignity and said he had nothing more to ask the witness. Of course, the public and the jury were left with a grain of doubt about a man who, while undergoing a certain cure, might have seen “the gates of heaven,” and who did not even know what year he lived in. But before Grigory left the stand, there was another episode. The President turned to the prisoner and asked if he wished to comment on the last witness’s evidence.

“All of it is true, except what he says about the door,” Mitya cried loudly. “I thank him for combing the lice off me, and I thank him for forgiving my blows. The old man has been honest all his life, and as faithful to my father as seven hundred poodles.”
“Prisoner, watch your language,” the President warned him.
“I am not a poodle,” Grigory muttered.
“Fine, I’m the poodle myself,” cried Mitya. “If it’s an insult, I’ll take it on myself, and I beg his pardon. I was a beast to him, and cruel. I was cruel to Æsop too.”
